name: Western Mambila
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible
sweep_summary: Western Mambila (nige1255) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Silbert & de Jong 2008 (JASA), is an acoustic study of American English fricatives (Crossref abstract read: 'American English fricatives in two prosodic contexts'); its Glottolog attachment to nige1255 is a mis-assignment and it is irrelevant. Beyond that item, I read three first-hand open papers by Bruce Connell on Mambila prosody (2004 TAL 'Tone, utterance length and F0 scaling', the 1996 'Four tones and downtrend' paper on the VIMS site, and the 2012 'Tones in tunes' chapter): all describe a four-level lexical tone system (Somié/Ba variety; most words monosyllabic; CV/CVC syllables) and none says anything about word stress, so no stress statement was found. The best unread candidates are Connell 2017 'Tone and Intonation in Mambila' (De Gruyter, 10.1515/9783110503524-005, pp. 131-166, paywalled), Perrin & Hill 1969 'Mambila (parler d'Atta): description phonologique' (print only), Connell 2006 ELL2 'Mambila' (Elsevier, paywalled) and Perrin 1974 in Ten Nigerian Tone Systems (SIL Jos, print). Connell 2007 (Persée) is nominally open but the PDF is behind an altcha wall; its readable first page is segmental.org, Wikipedia and mambila.info.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce (2004). Tone, utterance length and F0 scaling. In Proceedings of the International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2004), Beijing, 28-31 March 2004. ISCA Archive.
sources.quote: The present study examines Mambila, a Bantoid language spoken in the Nigeria-Cameroon borderland. Mambila has four level lexical tones High (H), Upper Mid (UM), Lower Mid (LM), and Low (L); previous work on tone in Mambila [8, 9, 10, 11] has shown that declination (in like-tone sequences) only reliably occurs with L. [...] Mambila syllable structure is simple, essentially either CV or CVC, with no clusters in either onset or coda, hence number of syllables is considered a valid measure of utterance length.
sources.locator: sec. 3 'F0 scaling and utterance length in Mambila' and sec. 3.1 Methodology (p. 1-2 of 3)
sources.note: First-hand phonetic study of F0 scaling in Mambila (Somié/Ba variety, five speakers). Describes a four-level lexical tone system and CV/CVC syllables; the word 'stress' occurs only in a cited title (Thorsen 1980). Silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2001. Downdrift, downstep, and declination. Paper, Typology of African Prosodic Systems Workshop, Bielefeld University, 18-20 May 2001. 8 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 3 'Downdrift in Mambila': four level tones, F0 data on downtrends (Somié/Ba variety, Cameroon side). No occurrence of stress, accent or prominence.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce (1996, revised). Four tones and downtrend: a preliminary report on pitch realization in Mambila, a language with four level tones. Revised version of a paper presented at ACAL 27 (Gainesville) and LAGB (Sussex) 1996. Online at the Virtual Institute of Mambila Studies.
sources.quote: Phonological research on Mambila tone has been done by Perrin (1974, n.d.). In her analysis, three units are required to describe tone in Mambila: the syllable, (phonological) word, and span. Every syllable bears at least one of four level tones which, in Perrin's system, are numbered from 1 to 4 (High to Low). [...] Possible tonal patterns - combinations or sequences of tones within the syllable - are limited to 2-1, 3-1, 4-1, 1-4, 2-4, 3-4, 2-1-4. These patterns appear to define the phonological word [...] Three syllable words in Mambila are uncommon, with the majority of words being monosyllabic.
sources.locator: sec. 2 (description of the Mambila tone system, following Perrin 1974)
sources.note: First-hand description of the Mambila (Somié, Ba) tone system and F0 downtrends by the language's principal describer; the words 'stress'/'accent' appear only in bibliography titles (Ladd & Johnson 1987). Silent on word stress; notes that most words are monosyllabic, which makes word-stress placement largely moot.

sources.citation: Perrin, Mona J. & Margaret V. Hill. 1969. Mambila (parler d'Atta): description phonologique. Yaoundé: Université Fédérale du Cameroun, Section de Linguistique Appliquée (SIL Cameroon 2008 IPA re-edition, 71 pp.).
sources.note: Sec. 2-4 'Le mot', p. 7 (p. 8): stress (accent d'intensité) falls on the first syllable except in disyllables ending in /a/, which stress the second syllable. Describes the ATTA dialect of Cameroon Mambila (came1252 / mcu), not the Nigerian variety nige1255.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce (2007). Mambila fricative vowels and Bantu spirantisation. Africana Linguistica 13: 7-31.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: In this paper I examine the fricative vowels of Len, a Mambila lect spoken just north of and adjacent to the Grassfields region of Cameroon. After a brief introduction to Len and relevant characteristics of its phonology, I review the phonetic structure of its fricative vowels, and present new evidence for their phonological characterisation.
sources.locator: Persée landing page, section 1 Introduction (PDF download is blocked by Persée's altcha proof-of-work; only the first page is in the landing HTML)
sources.note: Segmental (fricative-vowel) paper on the Len lect; the readable first page says nothing about stress and the paper's topic makes a stress statement unlikely. Nominally open (Persée) but the PDF endpoint refuses non-browser clients.

sources.note: Sec. 2 summarises Perrin's tone analysis (syllable / phonological word / span; four level tones; most words monosyllabic). Silent on stress.
